name: Mesotherapy

card.summary: Cocktail micro-injections into the skin, used for hair, skin and fat; supported by small studies in some uses, with limited standardisation and documented infection outbreaks from poor hygiene.
card.aka: Local intradermal therapy, LIT, biorejuvenation, hair mesotherapy, lipodissolve (fat variant)
card.note: Ingredients vary by practitioner; infections including atypical mycobacteria have been reported after non-sterile procedures.

quick.overview:
Mesotherapy means injecting small amounts of medications, vitamins, hyaluronic acid or other substances into the skin or just beneath it with fine needles. It was developed in France in 1952 by Michel Pistor, initially for pain, and later spread to cosmetic uses such as skin rejuvenation, hair loss and localised fat.

In looksmaxxing forums the term most often comes up for scalp mesotherapy alongside finasteride, dutasteride or minoxidil. Evidence is described as limited by small studies and non-standard mixtures, and expert bodies have not endorsed cosmetic fat removal.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say microinjections create a local depot that diffuses slowly, giving higher local concentrations with lower doses, and that the needle trauma itself stimulates repair. Reviews and critics note that the mixtures differ widely and that, for fat reduction, any effect may come from tissue damage by detergent-like ingredients.
quick.risks: Reported harms include injection-site infections, allergic reactions, tissue damage and inflammation. Outbreaks of rapidly growing mycobacteria followed mesotherapy and surgery in Brazil, and Australian clients developed abscesses. In the US the FDA cannot control what practitioners inject and state boards oversee the practice; only deoxycholic acid (Kybella) is approved for submental fat, and some countries restrict or ban cosmetic uses.

lead: Mesotherapy, also called local intradermal therapy (LIT), is a technique in which small doses of drugs, vitamins, minerals, enzymes, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts are injected through fine needles into the dermis or just beneath the skin. Its stated aim is localised action with minimal systemic exposure.[1][2] People use it to try to improve how skin, hair and body contour look: scalp injections for thinning hair, hydrating or revitalising mixtures for facial skin, and fat-dissolving mixtures for small deposits such as under the chin. A needle-free pressurised version delivers the ingredients with a jet of air.[2]

French physician Michel Pistor (1924-2003) is credited with developing it in 1952, initially using procaine injections for pain and vascular disorders; the term mesotherapy dates to 1958 and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a medical specialty in 1987.[1][2] Cosmetic uses developed later and include skin rejuvenation, hair loss and localised fat and cellulite treatment, and phosphatidylcholine injections became a distinct and controversial offshoot.[1][3]

The scientific record is mixed. A controlled study of a dutasteride-containing preparation in 126 women with pattern hair loss reported photographic improvement in 62.8 percent of treated patients versus 17.5 percent of saline controls, and the Italian Society of Mesotherapy has published a consensus supporting several indications.[7][8] Wikipedia, however, states that mesotherapy has no proven clinical efficacy and that cosmetic uses have generally not been tested in standard clinical trials, and critics quoted there include plastic surgeon Rod Rohrich.[2] Infection outbreaks have followed non-sterile practice.[4][5] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly for hair loss, in combination with finasteride, dutasteride and minoxidil.[6]

chain: Fine needles place small amounts of a mixture in or just under the skin
Local delivery to the scalp (or face, or fat deposit)
Scalp follicles exposed to drugs such as dutasteride; needle trauma may also prompt repair
Thicker-looking hair, or hydrated skin, depending on use
angle.text: Mesotherapy is used to deliver hair-loss drugs, vitamins or hyaluronic acid directly to the scalp or skin, with the aim of thicker hair or fresher-looking skin. In forums it is most often added to protocols built around finasteride, dutasteride and minoxidil.

paras: The method uses multiple shallow injections, typically no deeper than a few millimetres, over or near the target area, with small volumes of drug mixtures chosen by the practitioner.[1] Pistor summarised the approach as small volume, few times, in the right place.[1] Ingredients reported across practitioners include vitamins, enzymes, hyaluronic acid, procaine, dutasteride-containing preparations and, in some clinics, platelet-rich plasma.[2][7][10]

Wikipedia describes two techniques: standard injection with needles into the skin or subcutaneous tissue, and pressurised mesotherapy, which is needle-free and uses an accelerated jet of air to deliver ingredients; it cites a 2021 study by Maia and colleagues in which both reduced the fat layer, with better results from the pressurised method.[2] Sessions are repeated over weeks, and proponents say a local depot of the mixture diffuses slowly, giving higher local concentrations at lower doses, while the needle trauma itself may stimulate repair.[1]

Pistor first applied the technique to pain and vascular disorders in 1952; the French press coined the term in 1958, a French society was founded in 1964, and the Academie Nationale de Medecine recognised it in 1987.[1][2] It later spread through Europe, South America, Asia and the United States, notably for cosmetic fat reduction.[1][3] Wikipedia says it is practiced by about 18,000 physicians worldwide, a figure it tags as needing a citation.[2]

A 2006 review in Dermatologic Surgery sought to clarify the historical distinction between mesotherapy and the phosphatidylcholine injections popularised in Brazil.[3] An Italian society published a consensus report on its definition, rationale and clinical role in 2011.[8] In April 2011 France ratified a ban on mesotherapy for removing fat deposits after undesirable effects in the patients of one practitioner; the Conseil d'Etat cancelled it in June 2011, finding that the effects stemmed from unhygienic conditions rather than the treatment itself.[2]

Scalp mesotherapy is the use most discussed in appearance communities. A controlled study published in 2013 in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology enrolled 126 women with female pattern hair loss: 86 received 12 sessions of mesotherapy with a dutasteride-containing preparation and 40 controls received saline. At week 18 photographic improvement was seen in 62.8 percent of treated patients versus 17.5 percent of controls, hair pull and hair diameter measures improved, side effects were minor and similar between groups, and better results were linked to shorter disease duration.[7]

Grokipedia notes that systematic reviews as of 2024 describe promising results for hair loss but call for larger trials.[1] A registered retrospective study compared PRP with mesotherapy in androgenetic alopecia.[9] Dutasteride, finasteride and minoxidil are discussed in the wiki's separate entries and are the main drugs that appear in hair mesotherapy protocols.

Wikipedia reports that a 2006 study by Amin, Phelps and Goldberg gave 10 patients four monthly sessions of facial multivitamin mesotherapy and found no clinically relevant rejuvenation, while proponents describe hydration and collagen stimulation from hyaluronic acid and other substances.[1][2] The Italian Society of Mesotherapy consensus cites clinical benefit for facial skin aging among supported indications, and a laboratory study of activated PRP on human dermal fibroblasts, which notes PRP has been used clinically in mesotherapy, examined effects on extracellular matrix remodelling.[8][10] A prospective controlled study reported histologic evidence of new collagen after PRP in skin rejuvenation.[15]

Wikipedia states that no conclusive research shows any compound specifically targets fat cells, and that any effect might result from the detergent-like cell lysis of deoxycholic acid; Rod Rohrich of UT Southwestern is quoted as saying there is no data or science showing mesotherapy works, and Naomi Lawrence says phosphatidylcholine is not a benign drug.[2] A histology study examined tissue changes after mesotherapy for fat dissolution.[11]

The one product with approval is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), which the FDA approved in June 2015 for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin on the basis of a phase III trial of about 2,600 patients in which 68.2 percent responded and 81 percent had mild, temporary reactions such as bruising, swelling and pain.[2] It is not approved for other body areas.[2]

Grokipedia says randomised trials in musculoskeletal pain have shown reductions in pain and improved function.[1] The Italian consensus states that, when done correctly, intradermal therapy is considered a worthwhile option for regional painful conditions, and also lists chronic venous lymphatic insufficiency and oedematous fibrosclerotic panniculopathy among supported uses, while calling for larger trials.[8] Registered trials compare mesotherapy with other approaches in conditions such as lateral epicondylitis, knee osteoarthritis and chronic shoulder pain.[12][13][14]

Risks listed include infection, allergic reactions and tissue damage when procedures are non-sterile or done by unqualified practitioners.[1] An outbreak affecting 311 patients in Belem, Brazil, in 2004-2005 involved rapidly growing mycobacteria after laparoscopic surgery and other procedures; of 67 isolates studied, 8 came from mesotherapy patients and were identified as Mycobacterium bolletii, with molecular typing separating two concurrent outbreaks.[4] A new Mycobacterium species was described from a cosmetic infection and a nail salon.[5]

Wikipedia mentions an Australian salon investigated in 2008 after clients developed skin abscesses and one a mycobacterial infection, and a US dermatologist warned that phosphatidylcholine can cause unpredictable and severe inflammation.[2] The Italian consensus says mesotherapy should be used only after the patient understands its advantages and limitations and only by an experienced, qualified physician.[8]

Human studies include the controlled dutasteride mesotherapy study in 126 women with pattern hair loss,[7] a histology study of mesotherapy for fat dissolution,[11] a 10-patient facial multivitamin study described by Wikipedia,[2] and a prospective controlled study of PRP for collagen formation in skin rejuvenation.[15] Registered trials cover non-cosmetic uses such as lateral epicondylitis, knee osteoarthritis, myofascial pain and shoulder pain,[12][13][14][16] as well as facial scars with botulinum toxin and vitamin C mesotherapy for gingival pigmentation.[17][18] Grokipedia describes overall validation as limited by small samples, non-standard mixtures and few large randomised trials.[1]

In the United States the FDA cannot control what practitioners inject and state medical boards oversee the practice; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons has not endorsed mesotherapy and the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery said in 2005 that further study is needed.[2] Several South American countries ban it, Brazil has prohibited it for fat uses, and Italy restricts it to licensed medical professionals.[1][2]

A looksmax.org thread describes a user told by a hair transplant clinic that scalp mesotherapy plus an oral and topical drug regimen could thicken his hairline without a transplant, and asks others whether it would work.[6] In forums the term is mostly attached to hair-loss protocols that combine mesotherapy with finasteride or dutasteride and minoxidil.

Related procedures include microneedling, platelet-rich plasma injections, dermal fillers and botulinum toxin, all of which also deliver or stimulate through the skin; clinics sometimes combine them with mesotherapy.[10][15][17]

timeline.event: Michel Pistor develops mesotherapy using procaine injections for pain and vascular disorders.[1][2]
The term mesotherapy is coined by the French press.[1][2]
French Academy of Medicine recognises mesotherapy as a specialty.[1][2]
Mycobacterial outbreaks in Belem, Brazil begin, including mesotherapy patients.[4]
American Society for Dermatologic Surgery says further study is needed before endorsement.[2]
Dermatologic Surgery review clarifies mesotherapy versus phosphatidylcholine injections; 10-patient facial multivitamin study.[3][2]
Italian Society of Mesotherapy consensus report; France ratifies a fat-removal ban in April that the Conseil d'Etat cancels in June.[8][2]
Controlled study of dutasteride mesotherapy in 126 women with pattern hair loss published.[7]
FDA approves deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for submental fat.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org mesotherapy appears chiefly as a scalp treatment discussed alongside hair-loss drugs.[6]

claims.claim: Scalp mesotherapy can regrow or thicken hair and may replace a transplant.
claims.believers: A user relays a clinic's advice that mesotherapy plus drug changes could restore hairline thickness without a transplant.[6]
claims.experts: A controlled study in 126 women reported photographic improvement in 62.8 percent of treated patients versus 17.5 percent of controls, and Grokipedia says systematic reviews are promising but call for larger trials.[7][1]

claims.claim: Mesotherapy cocktails dissolve fat or rejuvenate skin.
claims.believers: Proponents describe hydration, collagen stimulation and fat breakdown from injected mixtures.[1][2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states cosmetic uses lack standard trials and that no conclusive research shows any compound targets fat cells, with a 10-patient facial study showing no clinically relevant benefit; the Italian consensus lists facial skin aging among supported uses.[2][8]

claims.claim: Mesotherapy is safe because it uses very small doses.
claims.believers: Proponents say low doses and local delivery reduce systemic exposure and side effects.[1]
claims.experts: Infection outbreaks including mycobacteria have been documented after non-sterile procedures, and a Brazilian outbreak included mesotherapy patients.[2][4]

claims.claim: Needle trauma from mesotherapy itself stimulates repair and rejuvenation.
claims.believers: Proponents say the micro-injury and the injected substances stimulate collagen and local healing.[1]
claims.experts: A prospective controlled study found histologic evidence of new collagen after PRP; a 10-patient multivitamin study found no clinically relevant rejuvenation.[15][2]

claims.claim: Mesotherapy is a recognised medical specialty.
claims.believers: Practitioners point to French Academy of Medicine recognition in 1987 and the Italian Society of Mesotherapy consensus.[1][8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states the technique has no proven clinical efficacy and the FDA does not regulate what practitioners inject, while the ASPS has not endorsed it.[2]

claims.claim: Injecting dutasteride into the scalp avoids the side effects of the oral drug.
claims.believers: Users describe dutasteride mesotherapy as part of a hair protocol and as a lower-exposure alternative to oral use.[6]
claims.experts: The 2013 study reported minor side effects not different from saline controls in women, and no study has compared it with the oral drug.[7]
